drills.q: Derive the ~36.8% out-of-bag fraction for bootstrap sampling and explain what it's used for.
drills.a: P(row never drawn in n draws with replacement from n rows) = (1-1/n)^n, which converges to 1/e ~ 0.368 as n grows. The excluded ~36.8% of rows per tree are usable as a free out-of-bag validation estimate without a separate holdout set.

drills.q: A LightGBM model overfits badly even though max_depth looks conservative. What's the likely cause and fix?
drills.a: Leaf-wise growth with an uncapped/high num_leaves grows one branch very deep regardless of max_depth's nominal limit -- max_depth alone doesn't bound leaf count for leaf-wise trees the way it does for level-wise growth. Fix: cap num_leaves explicitly, roughly below 2^max_depth, and tune the two jointly.

drills.q: A target-encoded categorical feature performs great in CV but degrades sharply in production. Diagnose and connect to CatBoost's fix.
drills.a: Naive target encoding computes each category's value using the full training set including the current row's own label -- CV run after this global encoding inherits the leakage, inflating CV performance. CatBoost's ordered target statistics fix this by encoding each row using only rows preceding it in a random permutation, so no row ever sees its own label in its encoding.

drills.q: A colleague claims 'gradient boosting always beats random forests.' Give a concrete counterexample and how you'd verify it on your own data.
drills.a: On data with heavy label noise, boosting's sequential residual-fitting can end up fitting the noise in later rounds, while random forest averaging is more robust since noisy per-tree errors partially cancel. Verify by fitting both with reasonable defaults and comparing validation performance directly -- an unstable-across-seeds or widening train/val gap for boosting is a concrete signal this dataset is in the exception case.

drills.q: Explain GOSS's reweighting factor (1-a)/b and why dropping low-gradient rows without reweighting would be wrong.
drills.a: GOSS keeps all top-a% high-gradient rows and samples a fraction b of the rest, multiplying the sampled low-gradient rows by (1-a)/b when computing gain. This keeps the expected gradient sum close to the full-data value; dropping without reweighting would systematically underestimate the aggregate contribution of low-gradient rows, biasing split selection.

drills.q: You have 50M rows, 200 mostly-numeric features, and a same-day training budget. Which library first, why, and what single experiment validates the choice?
drills.a: LightGBM first -- leaf-wise growth plus GOSS row subsampling target exactly this shape (large rows, numeric-heavy so EFB's categorical benefit matters less). Validate with a small-scale (2-5M row) timed comparison against XGBoost hist with matched effective capacity (num_leaves vs max_depth), since XGBoost's histogram adoption has narrowed the historical LightGBM speed gap and old benchmarks shouldn't be assumed to hold on this specific data/hardware.

drills.q: Derive XGBoost's closed-form leaf weight from the second-order Taylor approximation and explain what happens when a leaf has very few examples and lambda is small.
drills.a: w* = -sum(g_i)/(sum(h_i)+lambda), minimizing the 2nd-order Taylor-approximated loss for a fixed tree structure. With few examples, sum(h_i) is small, and a small lambda barely dampens the denominator, producing a large, unstable weight -- min_child_weight (minimum sum of Hessians per leaf) exists specifically to disallow splits creating such thinly-supported leaves.

drills.q: Explain CatBoost's 'prediction shift' and why it's distinct from ordinary train/test leakage from preprocessing.
drills.a: Prediction shift is internal to standard boosting: the residual for row i at round m comes from a model that already used row i's own label in earlier rounds, producing systematic optimism that compounds -- most pronounced on small datasets. This is distinct from a data-pipeline leak (e.g. global encoding computed on the full dataset including test rows), which is avoidable by strict train/test separation; prediction shift persists even with zero cross-set leakage unless the boosting algorithm itself guards against it, as ordered boosting does.
